questions.q: What are the constituent elements present in a molecule of pure water ($H_2O$)?
questions.a: The constituent elements are hydrogen and oxygen. A wrong answer shows that the student is confusing chemical compounds with physical mixtures or elements, often mistaking the name "water" for a single fundamental element rather than a combination of two gases.

questions.q: Why is table salt (sodium chloride, $NaCl$) classified as a compound rather than a mixture of sodium and chlorine?
questions.a: Table salt is a compound because its components, sodium and chlorine, are chemically combined in a fixed ratio, and it possesses entirely different properties from shiny sodium metal and poisonous chlorine gas. A wrong answer indicates that the student thinks components in compounds keep their individual physical properties like they do in mixtures.

questions.q: A student burns $12\text{ g}$ of carbon completely in oxygen to form $44\text{ g}$ of carbon dioxide ($CO_2$). Using the law of fixed proportions, how much oxygen gas reacted with the carbon?
questions.a:
Step 1: Identify the total mass of the compound formed ($44\text{ g}$ of $CO_2$).
Step 2: Identify the mass of the starting carbon element ($12\text{ g}$).
Step 3: Apply the conservation of mass / fixed proportion principle: Mass of oxygen = Total mass of compound - Mass of carbon.
Step 4: Calculate: $44\text{ g} - 12\text{ g} = 32\text{ g}$ of oxygen.
A wrong answer reveals that the student is adding the numbers together or does not understand that compounds have mass made strictly from their fixed constituent elements.

questions.q: Analyze the chemical formulas for water ($H_2O$), carbon dioxide ($CO_2$), and table salt ($NaCl$). What common feature do all three share regarding their elemental composition?
questions.a: All three are compounds consisting of two or more different elements combined in a fixed, definite atomic ratio. A wrong answer suggests the student views chemical formulas as arbitrary letters rather than precise representations of fixed elemental ratios in compounds.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Dissolving sugar in water creates a new compound because the sugar disappears and the water becomes sweet." Is this scientifically correct?
questions.a: The statement is incorrect because dissolving sugar in water forms a physical mixture (solution), not a new chemical compound; the sugar molecules retain their chemical identity and can be recovered by evaporating the water. A wrong answer shows confusion between physical dissolution (mixtures) and chemical combination (compounds).

questions.q: Design a simple home-based reasoning test to prove that table sugar ($C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$) is a compound and not an element. Describe what you would observe.
questions.a: A good answer would suggest heating white sugar strongly in a test tube; it decomposes into black carbon residue and water droplets on the container walls, proving it breaks down into multiple simpler substances. A poor answer relies merely on appearance or fails to show how compounds decompose into constituent elements.
